items.title: India is on the Move
items.summary:
When people talk about India’s economy, they almost always compare it negatively with China’s, it has not industrialized as fast, its bureaucracy is still maddening, its cities are still choked with traffic and smog. All true. But if you step back one of the greatest stories of the twenty-first century is unfolding: India, like China before it, is on the move.

India reached a GDP per capita of $10,039 in 2025, (PPP constant 2021 international dollars), nearly five times its 1990 level. India now has the same GDP per capita China had in late 2009! India has lagged behind China but by only about 15 years, approximately the time difference between Deng Xiaoping’s 1978 economic opening and India’s 1991 dismantling of the License Raj–a blink in historical time. 

Moreover, India is now growing faster than China. At 6% per-capita growth, living standards double every twelve years. Another decade and a half of this and India is a $20,000-per-capita middle-income country, looking more like today’s Brazil or Mexico than the India of Mother Theresa.

Indeed, India’s growth has already greatly reduced the worst forms of poverty, as China’s growth did previously. Extreme poverty in India fell from 47.5 percent in 1993—and 27.1 percent as recently as 2011—all the way down to 2.6 percent in 2023 (using the World Bank’s extreme poverty line, $3.00 a day in 2021 PPP). Hundreds of millions of people climbed out of destitution in a single generation.

Visiting India, you can see the transformation in daily life. In 2000, four in ten Indians lacked electricity and nearly three-quarters…
items.t: India is on the Move

items.title: The mental illness theory of politics is modestly underrated
items.summary:
Using a large national panel dataset, we find that receiving counseling from mental health professionals decreases the likelihood of protesting in subsequent weeks by 34%–39%. Experimental results are broadly consistent with observational findings. In a field experiment, mental health outreach reduces anxiety by an average of 11% ( d = 0.41), with mediation analyses showing decreased anxiety is related to a decrease in interest in political engagement. In a survey experiment, higher anxiety is related to greater odds of volunteering.

That is from a recent piece by Elaine K. Denny, and Melissa N. Baker, via the excellent Kevin Lewis .

items.title: HumanFish — Predicting Who Actually Wins a Human Chess Game
items.summary:
The eval bar on a chess broadcast answers the wrong question. It tells you what happens if two 3600-Elo engines play perfectly with infinite time. What you actually want to know while watching humans play is: who is going to win from here, how likely is a draw, and why? 

HumanFish is an open hybrid model trained on 550,001 tournament positions (91,720 human 2400–2900 games) combining Stockfish 19 , Leela Chess Zero , a grandmaster move predictor ( DSC-150M ), and live tournament clocks . It outputs calibrated White Win / Draw / Black Win odds—and shows the concrete moves behind every disagreement right on the board.

I have long wanted such a thing, here is the link .  Built by the well-known book reviewer Patrick Collison .

The post HumanFish — Predicting Who Actually Wins a Human Chess Game appeared first on Marginal REVOLUTION .

items.title: David Collard obituary
items.summary:
My friend and colleague David Collard, who has died aged 89, was an economist of unusual breadth: a theorist steeped in the history of ideas who never accepted that people act from self-interest alone.

Based at the University of Bath for nearly 25 years, he joined as professor of economics in 1978, becoming emeritus in 2002. He led the political economy group for 16 years (which later evolved into the economics department), headed the school of social sciences, and served as pro-vice-chancellor from 1989 to 1992. In those roles, he did much to raise the standing of the social sciences in a university built on science and engineering.

items.title: What we are grateful for
items.summary:
Here is The Free Press symposium .  Here is an excerpt from my piece, which has a chance of turning out to be prescient by a day:

Since I was born in 1962, what has been the biggest fundamental theoretical breakthrough? We put a man on the moon and built the internet, but what about on a theoretical level? The standard model of particle physics, from the 1960s and 1970s, is one candidate. Still, the early 20th century was more exciting for theory.

We still lack a theory of quantum gravity, and string theory looks less likely with time. The fundamentals of economics, my own field, have barely changed, even as our empirical knowledge has grown. Now I have more hope for some thrilling new theories, aided by both man and machine.

Just last night Ven Chandrasekaran and Astra dropped a new (and not yet confirmed) theory of quantum gravity .

items.title: Five Facts About Stablecoins
items.summary:
We document five facts about payment stablecoins using wallet-level blockchain data from 2020 to 2025. First, stablecoins serve as a transaction currency: onchain volume exceeds Bitcoin’s despite a much smaller supply, velocity has risen sharply, and transactions have shifted toward low-value transfers. Second, using transaction timing to refine exchange-based attribution, we find activity spread across the Americas, Europe, and Asia and fewer cross-regional flows than the standard method implies. Third, we estimate a structural cash-management model on the holdings data and find that the costs of accessing stablecoin wallets have fallen since 2023. Fourth, stablecoins are becoming the settlement currency of a fast-growing onchain credit market, and their growth appears to reallocate rather than destroy credit. Fifth, smart contracts are involved in about a third of Ethereum stablecoin transactions and over two thirds of volume, and protocols such as x402 demonstrate sub-cent machine-to-machine payments. Stablecoins behave as tokenized money, with implications for financial markets and regulation.

That is from a recent NBER working paper by Lin William Cong , Gordon Y. Liao , Eswar S. Prasad & Tony Zhang . 

The post Five Facts About Stablecoins appeared first on Marginal REVOLUTION .

items.title: How did the United States become a lawyerly society?
items.summary:
Between 1970 and 1990 the U.S. legal services industry underwent a dramatic demand shift. Its employment share more than doubled and the relative wages of lawyers rose by 60%, in contrast to stability before and after. We attribute this shift to three related changes in the legal environment: a wave of new legislation and regulation broadened the scope of the law, left its application uncertain, and enlisted private lawyers to enforce it through fee-shifting. Using over a century of data, we show that lawyers’ employment and compensation track all three changes. Event studies link specific statutes to increased litigation and demand for the affected fields of law. Other explanations, including lawyer quality, industrial composition, and technology, do not account for the demand shift. We estimate that legislative uncertainty accounts for roughly 13% of the demand shift—a cost of about $23 billion in 2024 alone.

That is from a new paper by Ariell Resheff and Cailin Slattery.  Via Krzysztof Tyszka-Drozdowski . 

The post How did the United States become a lawyerly society? appeared first on Marginal REVOLUTION .

items.title: Avoiding disempowerment through protectionism?
items.summary:
Recently many people are debating whether AI will lead to our disempowerment.  One simple example is that we might use AI to pursue or solve various intellectual tasks for us, rather than doing it ourselves.

So say there are twenty important math problems, and we let the AIs (with some human guidance) take a crack at them.  Say the AIs solve seventeen of those problems, the humans one, and two remain unsolved.

Alternately, say we ban or limit AIs, and over a longer period of time the humans solve three of those problems.  The rest go unsolved.

Arguably in the latter situation the humans are exercising more agency and, as unaided humans, achieving greater things.  But in the former situation there is more discovery, possibly more usefulness, and the marginal impact of total human effort (including building the AIs) is far greater.

Which scenario involves greater “disempowerment”?  I do not view the concept of disempowerment as entirely well defined, but it seems to my virgin eyes that the humans are more “disempowered” in the latter case, where only three of the problems get solved.

And take those two extra problems that get solved (eventually) by humans.  Should we feel empowered if we achieve two theorem proofs due to what you might call protectionism, or how about labeling it “DEI for humans”?

Say I was working on a difficult economics problem, and I learned that an unpublished manuscript from China had solved the problem.  But no one else knows about the manuscript, except for me that is.  I could announce the manuscript and give it full credit.  Or I could ignore…
items.t: Avoiding disempowerment through protectionism?

items.title: Gambling for Goals
items.summary:
Young adults in advanced economies have grown more pessimistic about their economic prospects in recent years. At the same time, gambling-like financial activities have proliferated. We link these trends through a Friedman-Savage (1948) motive: when life goals such as homeownership or marriage seem out of reach, individuals turn to financial gambles. We test this theory using an original survey combined with millions of linked records from Korea’s leading credit bureau, telecom provider, and credit card issuer. Consistent with the theory, individuals who place greater importance on hard-to-reach goals take more risk, and the form of risk they take varies systematically with their distance from those goals. Within individuals, cryptocurrency app usage rises during unemployment and falls after winning the right to purchase price-regulated housing through a lottery. A calibration shows how hard-to-reach goals lead households to act more aggressively on their beliefs, amplifying the consequences of overoptimism.

That is from a new NBER working paper by Costas Arkolakis , Spencer Y. Kwon , Dominic Russel , Claire Shi & Hyunjoo Yang .

items.title: Best fiction 2026
items.summary:
This year brought a remarkably strong showing in fiction.  Here is my list in the order I read them:

Siri Hustvedt, Ghost Stories: A Memoir .

Karl Knausgaard, The School of Night .

Juan Marsé, Last Evenings with Teresa  [new translation]

Claudia Piñeiro, Cathedrals .

Christian Kracht, Eurotrash [2025], and Air [2026].

Munir Hachemi, The Mulai .

Egana Djabbarova, My Dreadful Body .

China Mieville, The Rouse (still reading this one).

Ingeborg Bachmann and Max Frisch, ‘We Didn’t Do Very Well’: The Correspondence .  Here are my remarks on the German-language edition .

Adolo Bioy Casares, Morel’s Invention , new translation by Margaret Jull Costa.

Missouri Williams, The Vivisectors .

Mathias Enard, Perfecting the Shot .

M. John Harrison, The End of Everything .

Solvej Ball, On the Calculation of Volume V , noting you cannot start at the fifth volume for this series.

There is also a new Min Lee novel, and a new and short Jon Fosse novel, as possible contenders for this list.  I have not yet read them.  As for a “best of,” the Knausgaard and the Bachmann-Frisch correspondence stand out for me, Bioy Casares as well.

What else?  I do believe we are entering an era where high quality fiction is more and more important.  I am delighted to see that our writers and translators are responding accordingly.
